proxy_language: Kiedtra is not a known historical culture; it is a fictional/game-internal culture whose existing names look like a Goidelic/Germanic/Finnic hybrid. The only defensible proxy for a 'later court' culture situated in Rodos (Rhodes) is Medieval/Koine-descended Greek as spoken on Rhodes under the Knights Hospitaller era court (Medieval/Late Byzantine and Dodecanese Greek), transliterated in a standard scholarly romanization.
proxy_rationale: No attested language 'Kiedtra' exists; no scholarly literature supports it. Because the assigned region is Rodos and the period index is R (late/court period), the most defensible real-language anchor is Medieval Greek of Rhodes (Byzantine to Hospitaller period, c. 11th-15th c.). The link is purely geographic and nominal: the name Kiedtra itself and the current game strings (Rusu-, -kurrak, -teoil-) do not derive from Greek. Treat the proxy as a naming-style scaffold, not a claim about the culture's real language. Note that Rhodian Greek and Dodecanesian dialects preserve some Medieval features (e.g. palatalization of k before front vowels to ts/tsh, lack of final -n in some forms).
phonology: Medieval/Early Modern Greek (Rhodian) phoneme inventory. Vowels: /i e a o u/ (iotacism: eta, iota, upsilon, ei, oi all merge to /i/; ai > /e/; omega/omicron > /o/; ou > /u/). Consonants: stops /p t k b d g/ (b d g from voiced stops/postnasal), fricatives /f v th(theta) dh(delta) s z x gh(gamma)/, affricates /ts dz/, nasals /m n/, liquids /l r/, glides via palatalization. Southeastern dialects (Dodecanesian) have palatalization of /k/ and /x/ before front vowels (>/c/, /tsh/ or /sh/), final-n retention, and unstressed high-vowel loss (apocope/syncope) in northern dialects but not in Rhodes where vowels are largely preserved. Stress is word-based (dynamic) and falls on one of the last three syllables.
phonotactics: Syllables are (C)(C)V(C) with open syllables strongly preferred; word-final consonants are restricted to -s, -n (and -r in some learned/foreign words), with -s the commonest (nominative -os, -is, -as, -es). Onset clusters allowed: stop+liquid (pr, tr, kr, pl, kl, gl, br, dr, gr), fricative+liquid (fr, thr, ghr, vr), s+stop (sk, st, sp), s+nasal (sm), stop+s? no; ps, ks as single onsets; nasal+stop medially (mp, nt, nk, ngk). Medial geminates are rare (spelled but pronounced single in most dialects except Dodecanese, where gemination is preserved: -ll-, -tt-, -ss-, -kk-). Vowel hiatus is common (ea, ia, io, oi). Stress does not change spelling in transliteration if diacritics are omitted; scholarly practice marks stress with an acute only in reconstructions.
orthography: Use a simple ELOT/ISO-843-style Latin transliteration: a e i o u, b d g k l m n p r s t v z, f, th (theta), dh (delta), gh (gamma), kh/ch (chi), ps, ks (xi) as 'ks', ts, dz, ng/gk for gamma-kappa, mp for mu-pi, nt for nu-tau, y for upsilon only in classical-style spelling (otherwise i). Digraphs: ai=e, ei=i, oi=i, ou=u, ei and oi may be kept in learned spelling. No h except in th/kh/gh/ch/sh. Omit diacritics and stress marks in game names.
morphology: Greek is fusional and inflecting. Nouns: three genders (m/f/n), two numbers, four cases in the Medieval/Modern system (nominative, genitive, accusative, vocative; dative lost, replaced by se + accusative or genitive). Declension classes: masc -os/-is/-as/-es, fem -a/-i/-o/-is, neuter -o/-i/-ma/-os. Genitive sg: -u (masc/neut -os/-o), -s (fem -a/-i: -as/-is), pl -on. Adjectives agree in gender, number, case and precede the noun. Verbs: stem + person/number endings with augment and reduplication in older forms. Derivational suffixes: -tis/-tir (agent), -ma (result), -sis (action), -ia (abstract/place), -on (place/diminutive), -aki/-itsa (diminutive), -eion/-eio (place where, e.g. fanari-eio), -ikos (adjective).
compounding: Greek compounds are head-final: modifier + linking vowel -o- + head (e.g. thalass-o-kratia). First element takes the combining form (stem + -o-); if the second element begins with a vowel the -o- is dropped (e.g. psar-a-... no: pyrg-o-... but arkh-i-...). 'X of Y' names are expressed either by genitive: head noun + Y in genitive (o naos tu iliu, 'temple of the sun'; transliterated game name could be naos iliu) or by compound (iliotemplo no; iliovasilion no). 'Y-maker' is formed with -poios/-piis/-ergos or the agent suffix -tis: artopoios (bread-maker), psaras (fisherman), kanonis? Use stem + -tis / -poios. Place names often use -ia, -ion, -polis, -khori(on), or Saint-names (Ayios).
noun_phrase_order: Adjective + noun (kalos anthropos); article precedes the noun phrase (o, i, to; I omit it in names); genitive follows the head noun (o naos tu theu); demonstratives and possessives precede or follow depending on emphasis; in compounds the modifier precedes the head.

notes: Kiedtra is not an attested culture and its current game names are not Greek; this proxy is a geographic fallback (Rodos = Rhodes) and should be flagged as speculative. If designers intend Kiedtra to be a fully invented language, names should instead be generated from a documented conlang ruleset, not presented as a real language. No word may be identical to a Modern Irish, Scottish Gaelic or Manx word, since Greek is not Goidelic; a post-filter should reject any generated name matching a Goidelic dictionary entry (e.g. avoid ending names in -ag, -ach, -an with Goidelic roots such as caisteal, mara, uisce, or Gaelic-looking sequences like 'teoil' and 'kurrak' seen in current game names).
